title: Distributed transactions
lead: Distributed locking, global deadlocks, two-phase commit and recovery.

sections.title: Partitioned data and distributed locking
sections.html:
A distributed transaction accesses data on multiple nodes while presenting one transaction to the application. This lecture assumes shared-nothing nodes with partitioned, nonreplicated data. A coordinator organises each transaction’s work.

Locks can be partitioned with the data so each node manages locks for its local objects. Coarser objects spanning nodes can have a designated home lock manager or a central manager.

Local lock correctness does not settle global deadlock or atomic commitment. Every participating node must agree on whether the transaction commits, including when nodes or messages fail.

PDF pp. 1–12

sections.title: Global deadlocks and commitment
sections.html:
A waits-for cycle may span nodes even when every local graph is acyclic. Combining local dependencies can reveal a global cycle; aborting an appropriate victim breaks it. Distributed detection must account for information that can be delayed.

Commit has a different requirement: every participant must be ready. A local constraint violation or abort vote prevents a global commit. Missing messages and crashed nodes make collecting and disseminating the decision difficult.

Timeouts indicate that progress or communication is missing; they do not by themselves prove what a remote node has durably decided. This distinction drives the logging requirements of two-phase commit.

PDF pp. 13–21

sections.title: Two-phase commit protocol
sections.html:
In phase 1, the coordinator sends PREPARE and gathers YES/NO votes. A participant voting YES promises it can commit later and must not independently abandon that prepared transaction. Commit requires YES from all participants.

In phase 2, the coordinator sends the global COMMIT or ABORT decision. Participants apply that decision and acknowledge it. Two-phase commit (2PC) decides transaction outcome; two-phase locking (2PL) controls conflicting access. They solve different problems.

If the coordinator cannot obtain all required votes before deciding, it can abort. Once a commit decision is durable, retrying communication must preserve that decision.

PDF pp. 22–30

sections.title: Persistent protocol state
sections.html:
Before voting YES, a participant flushes its PREPARE record and the recovery information needed to fulfil that promise. Before announcing COMMIT, the coordinator flushes the decision and records the participant identities needed for recovery.

Participants log and persist the received decision before acknowledging as required by the presented protocol. The coordinator records completion after collecting acknowledgements. The source marks forced log records with an asterisk to show message-order dependencies.

These records allow a restarted process to distinguish an undecided transaction from a decided one. A message sent without the required preceding flush could otherwise report a decision that disappears after a crash.

PDF pp. 31–48

sections.title: Recovery, strict locking and blocking
sections.html:
A recovered coordinator with a durable commit decision resumes phase 2 if acknowledgements are incomplete. A prepared participant without a final decision must inquire and wait for reliable decision information. The source’s presumed-abort rules depend on the process’s role and log state.

Strict locking keeps uncertain transactions’ locks until their outcome is resolved. The source also orders messages per sender/receiver/transaction so a receiver does not process a later operation before missing earlier work.

2PC can block when a prepared participant cannot learn the coordinator’s decision. A timeout cannot safely choose between commit and abort in that state. Replicated commit protocols address additional failure cases; their details are outside this lecture.

PDF pp. 49–57

quiz.question: A participant has only a durable PREPARE record and loses contact with the coordinator. What is safe?
options: Commit independently because it voted YES
Abort immediately when a timeout expires
Seek the decision; it may have to wait
Delete the log and start over
quiz.explanation: A YES vote is a promise to follow the common decision. The coordinator may already have committed elsewhere.

source.summary: Lecture 22 studies partitioned, nonreplicated data, distributed locking, global deadlock, two-phase commit, and the coordination of logging with recovery. Two-phase commit can block progress when the coordinator is unreachable.

limitations: The lecture assumes partitioning without replication. Consensus-based improvements are mentioned but not developed in detail.
